title: 道德經 第二十四章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 24, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 64. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 24 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 苦恩 (Kindness Turned Bitter). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to stretch up on tiptoe (the graph is 人 'a man' above 止 'foot')
to stand — to have a footing that holds

sentences.l: One who goes on tiptoe does not stand;
sentences.n: The paradox is in the two verbs: to make yourself tall you leave off standing. Two notes on the text. In the Mawangdui silk manuscripts this chapter does not stand here at all — it comes earlier, before chapter 22 — which is one of the clearest signs that the order of the eighty-one chapters is an editor's and not the author's. And the character the manuscripts write at the head of this line is read by their editors as 炊 chuī, 'to puff, to blow', which would give 'one who puffs himself up does not stand'. Our edition prints 企 and we keep it.

sentences.t:
跨者不行，
自見者不明，
自是者不彰，
自伐者無功，
自矜者不長。
其在道也，
曰餘食贅行。

morph.gloss: to walk, to get anywhere (xíng; read háng it is a row or a trade)
himself — the reflexive object, before its verb as always
shows, puts on display (xiàn, not jiàn 'sees')
takes as right — the demonstrative used as a verb
makes much of, stands on his own worth
lasts long (cháng; zhǎng would be 'takes the lead')
these — the pronoun taken up as the topic of what follows
(the particle that closes a topic: 'as for ——')
are called — 曰 introduces the name given to a thing
left over, more than was wanted
food (shí; read sì it is 'to feed another')
tacked on and good for nothing — properly a wen, a lump of flesh the body carries and has no use for
conduct, the way a man carries himself — the sense Wang Bi keeps; many readers take the graph as standing for 形 xíng 'bodily form' instead, giving 'a growth on the body', and both words are read xíng

sentences.i: Straddle, and you get nowhere. Make a show of yourself and you are not seen; insist you are right and you do not stand out; vaunt yourself and the credit is not yours; make much of yourself and you do not last. Measured by the Way, such things are called scraps left on the plate, and behaviour a man carries about with him to no purpose.
sentences.n: Four of these lines are chapter 22's four, turned inside out: there 不自見故明, here 自見者不明. The book states the rule and then states its contrary, and the pair belong together whatever order the chapters ended up in. 見 is read xiàn, 'to show', as in chapter 22. The last two characters are a knot. Our edition prints 行 'walking, conduct', and Wang Bi reads it that way — his comment measures the man by his 行, his conduct, and brings in the 疣贅, the wen, as a comparison rather than as the word on the page. So the English here says conduct, and 贅 carries the wen in its own meaning: something the body grows, keeps, and has no use for. Many readers since have taken the graph instead as standing for 形 'bodily form', making 贅行 an actual growth of flesh. Happily both words are read xíng, so the line sounds the same either way; only the picture changes. 餘食 is food left after everyone has eaten: not a delicacy but the thing scraped off the plate.

sentences.t:
物或惡之，
故有道者不處。

morph.gloss: there are some that — not the modern Mandarin 'or'
to loathe, to find disgusting (wù; read è the character is 'ugly', as in chapter 2)
to dwell in, to take one's place in (chǔ; read chù it is a place)

sentences.l:
There are creatures that loathe them,
and so one who holds the Way does not dwell in them.
sentences.i: There is always something that finds such things loathsome, and so the man who holds the Way will have no part in them.
sentences.n: Both of the closing verbs have been met before, and in the same line: chapter 8 said of water 處眾人之所惡, 'it dwells in what the crowd loathes'. Set the two side by side and they look opposite — dwell in what is loathed, do not dwell in what is loathed — but the loathing is not the same. There it is people's distaste for the low place; here it is the revulsion any creature feels at what is superfluous and spoiled. 或 is the classical 'some, there are those who', and a trap: in modern Chinese the same character means 'or'.
